There is a particular kind of silence that hangs in a room where someone is waiting. It is not the silence of emptiness, but the silence of anticipation—a taut, humming thing, like a wire stretched between two points. I have been thinking about waiting lately. Not the impatient, foot-tapping brand of waiting that we do at traffic lights or in grocery store lines, but the deeper, more patient kind that we seem to have lost the vocabulary for. The kind that involves sitting with the unknown, without the urge to fill every gap with noise or distraction.

I remember, as a child, waiting for the mail. This was in the era before email, before the constant vibration of a phone, before information arrived with the instantaneity of lightning. My grandfather lived in another country, and he wrote letters on thin, blue airmail paper, the kind that was so translucent you could almost read the words before opening the envelope. The wait for those letters was an event. It could take two weeks, sometimes three. I would watch the postman from the window, my heart leaping at the sight of his blue uniform, then sinking when he walked past our gate without stopping. The wait was not passive; it was a kind of active hoping. I rehearsed what I would write back. I imagined his hands holding my reply. The letter, when it finally arrived, was more than words on a page—it was a distilled essence of all that waiting, a small miracle that had crossed an ocean.

We have largely lost that. The ability to wait, I mean. We have become intolerant of any lag, any delay. Streaming services buffer for a second and we fume. A text message goes unread for an hour and we wonder if we’ve been slighted. We have engineered our world to eliminate waiting, and in doing so, we have eliminated something essential about the rhythm of human experience. Waiting is not a bug; it is a feature. It is the darkroom in which certain images develop.

Consider the simple act of boiling water. I cook often, and I’ve noticed that the most impatient cooks are always lifting the lid, checking the pot, nudging the heat. But water boils when it boils. You cannot force it. There is a physics to it, a patience required. The water doesn't care about your schedule. It must absorb the heat, molecule by molecule, until it reaches that critical point. The wait is not empty; it is a process of transformation. The same is true for bread. You cannot rush the rise. The yeast works at its own pace, feeding on the sugars, releasing carbon dioxide, slowly inflating the dough into something airy and alive. If you rush it, you get a dense, leaden loaf. The wait is part of the recipe.

But we are not only waiting for physical processes. We wait for emotional ones. We wait for grief to soften, for a wound to heal, for a heartache to fade into something bearable. There is no app for that. You cannot download closure. You must sit with it, day after day, watching as the sharp edges of memory slowly become smooth. I have a friend who lost her husband two years ago. She told me that the hardest part was not the immediate aftermath—the shock, the funeral, the flood of condolences—but the long, slow second year, when everyone else had moved on and she was still waiting for the pain to become something she could carry. She said that waiting felt like drowning at first, and then, slowly, like learning to swim. She did not rush it. She let the waves come. She learned to wait.

There is also the waiting that happens in creative work. I write, and I am often asked about inspiration. The truth is that inspiration is not a lightning strike; it is a long, patient wait. You sit at the desk. You write bad sentences. You delete them. You stare out the window. You feel like a fraud. And then, sometimes, after hours of this—after the mind has exhausted its trivialities—something else emerges. A phrase you didn't know you had. An idea that feels like it came from somewhere else entirely. But you cannot schedule that moment. You can only prepare for it by showing up, by doing the work, by being willing to wait. The waiting is not the absence of creativity; it is the gestation of it.

I think this is why we are so uncomfortable with waiting. In a culture that worships productivity, waiting feels like failure. It feels like wasted time. But what if waiting is not wasted? What if it is the very soil in which meaning grows? The Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh wrote about the practice of "walking meditation," where you simply walk, paying attention to each step, not trying to get anywhere. That is a form of waiting—waiting for nothing in particular, just being present in the moment. And perhaps that is the deepest kind of waiting: the willingness to be here now, without craving a different now.

There is a famous story about the Buddha. A man asked him, "What have you gained through meditation?" The Buddha replied, "Nothing." Then he said, "But let me tell you what I have lost: anger, anxiety, depression, insecurity, fear of old age and death." The waiting, the silent sitting, the patient observation of breath and thought—it was not a gaining, but a losing. A stripping away. And that is what true waiting can be. It is a way of shedding our illusion of control. It is a surrender to the fact that some things cannot be hurried.

I am trying to practice this. When I am in a line at the store, I try not to pull out my phone. I just stand there. I look at the person in front of me. I notice the texture of the ceiling tiles. I breathe. It feels strange, almost rebellious, to simply wait. But after a few minutes, something settles. The frantic, restless energy that always buzzes in my chest quiets down. I remember that I am a human being, not a human doing. And there is a peace in that.

Of course, not all waiting is voluntary. There is the waiting of the hospital waiting room, the waiting for test results, the waiting for a phone call that could change everything. That kind of waiting is excruciating. It is a raw, raw place. But even there, I have seen something. I have seen people hold hands. I have seen strangers offer tissues. I have seen the shared silence of a room full of people who are all waiting for something, and who have, for a moment, dropped their masks. That waiting is not empty; it is full of fellow feeling. It reminds us that we are not alone in our waiting.

In the end, waiting is not the opposite of living. It is a profound part of living. It is the space between the question and the answer, between the seed and the sprout, between the beginning and the end. We cannot escape it. We can only choose how we inhabit it. We can fill it with frantic distraction, or we can let it work in us. We can curse the delay, or we can listen to what the delay is trying to teach us.

I think my grandfather knew this. He never complained about the time it took for letters to cross the ocean. He simply wrote, and he waited. And when the reply came, he savored it, as if the waiting had made it sweeter. I want to live like that. I want to be a person who can wait—not because I have nothing to do, but because I understand that the waiting is part of the doing. The slow, quiet, invisible work of becoming. So I will wait. I will wait for the water to boil. I will wait for the bread to rise. I will wait for the pain to soften. I will wait for the words to come. And I will trust that, in the waiting, something is being made.
